claim: Formation of the skin barrier requires rapid proliferation coupled with differentiation and stratification of the embryonic epidermis.
source: Formation of the skin barrier requires rapid proliferation coupled with differentiation and stratification of the embryonic epidermis.
evidence: This is a general statement about epidermal development that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Basal progenitors give rise to intermediate cells, a transient proliferative suprabasal cell population.
source: Basal progenitors give rise to progeny throughout development – first to intermediate cells, a transient proliferative suprabasal cell population, and later to spinous cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript including EdU staining and live imaging experiments.

claim: Basal progenitors later give rise to spinous cells.
source: Basal progenitors give rise to progeny throughout development – first to intermediate cells, a transient proliferative suprabasal cell population, and later to spinous cells.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments and temporal analysis of cell populations.

claim: Intermediate cells express a subset of genes in common with granular cells of the epidermis.
source: Further, we found that intermediate cells express a subset of genes in common with granular cells of the epidermis – the terminal living cell type that helps establish the barrier.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data and Gene Ontology analysis showing overlap between IC and granular cell gene signatures.

claim: Granular cells are the terminal living cell type that helps establish the barrier.
source: Further, we found that intermediate cells express a subset of genes in common with granular cells of the epidermis – the terminal living cell type that helps establish the barrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge about granular cell function in the epidermis.

claim: Most intermediate cells directly transition to granular cells without expressing markers specific to spinous cells.
source: Lineage tracing revealed that most intermediate cells directly transition to granular cells without expressing markers specific to spinous cells, thus revealing a distinct lineage pathway leading to granular fate.
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase lineage tracing experiments using K10-rtTA;TRE-H2B-GFP mice.

claim: Intermediate and granular cells both have hallmarks of increased actomyosin contractility.
source: In addition to their transcriptional similarities, intermediate and granular cells both had hallmarks of increased actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining of F-actin, Myosin IIA, and α18, as well as RNA-Seq data showing upregulation of contractility genes.

claim: Contractility is sufficient to suppress spinous fate and promote granular gene expression.
source: We found that rather than simply lying downstream of cell fate pathways, contractility was sufficient to suppress spinous fate and promote granular gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using K10-Spastin and K10-Arhgef11CA mouse models that induce contractility.

claim: Basal cells divide to generate spinous cells, which are postmitotic.
source: Subsequently, basal cells divide to generate spinous cells, which are postmitotic.
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data and live imaging showing lack of proliferation in spinous cells.

claim: Spinous cells differentiate into granular cells.
source: These cells then further differentiate into granular cells, the last living cell types in the epidermis which are integral to forming the epidermal barrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epidermal differentiation pathways.

claim: Intermediate cells are a transient cell type that expresses differentiation markers like keratin 1 (K1) and K10 but remain mitotically active.
source: ICs are a transient cell type that expresses differentiation markers like keratin 1 (K1) and K10 but remain mitotically active (Weiss and Zelickson, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation and confirmed by EdU incorporation data in the manuscript.

claim: At E14.5, the proliferation rate of intermediate cells is comparable to basal cells.
source: At this time point, the proliferation rate of ICs is comparable to basal cells, suggesting that they are a significant contributor to tissue expansion (Damen et al., 2021; Smart, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations and EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Intermediate cells are a significant contributor to tissue expansion.
source: At this time point, the proliferation rate of ICs is comparable to basal cells, suggesting that they are a significant contributor to tissue expansion (Damen et al., 2021; Smart, 1970).
evidence: This is inferred from the high proliferation rate of ICs.

claim: Intermediate cells lack basement membrane attachment.
source: These cells lack basement membrane attachment and, thus, they proliferate in a tissue environment that is normally quiescent in the adult.
evidence: This is established knowledge about intermediate cells and their position in the suprabasal layer.

claim: Intermediate cells proliferate in a tissue environment that is normally quiescent in the adult.
source: These cells lack basement membrane attachment and, thus, they proliferate in a tissue environment that is normally quiescent in the adult.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between embryonic and adult epidermis.

claim: Generation of intermediate cells is transient (E14–15.5).
source: Generation of ICs is transient (E14–15.5), and by E16.5 basal cells give rise to postmitotic spinous cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis of cell populations shown in Figure 1.

claim: By E16.5 basal cells give rise to postmitotic spinous cells.
source: Generation of ICs is transient (E14–15.5), and by E16.5 basal cells give rise to postmitotic spinous cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data and live imaging experiments.

claim: Increased contractility in differentiated cells of the epidermis results in a non-cell autonomous effect on proliferation of their progenitors.
source: Further, increased contractility in differentiated cells of the epidermis results in a non-cell autonomous effect on proliferation of their progenitors (Ning et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The proliferation rate of suprabasal cells decreases from E14.5 to E16.5.
source: The proliferation rate of suprabasal cells decreases over the next 48 hr, and these cells are largely postmitotic by E16.5.
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Suprabasal cells are largely postmitotic by E16.5.
source: The proliferation rate of suprabasal cells decreases over the next 48 hr, and these cells are largely postmitotic by E16.5.
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data and live imaging experiments.

claim: All divisions visualized in suprabasal cells were planar to the epithelium.
source: All divisions visualized were planar to the epithelium.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from live imaging experiments.

claim: Biological replicates grouped together in principal component analysis.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the sequenced cell populations revealed that biological replicates grouped together and that samples were segregated by cell type (basal vs suprabasal) in the first component, and by age in the second component (E14.5 vs E16.5).
evidence: This is shown in the PCA plot in Figure 1E.

claim: Samples were segregated by cell type (basal vs suprabasal) in the first principal component.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the sequenced cell populations revealed that biological replicates grouped together and that samples were segregated by cell type (basal vs suprabasal) in the first component, and by age in the second component (E14.5 vs E16.5).
evidence: This is shown in the PCA plot in Figure 1E.

claim: Samples were segregated by age in the second principal component.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the sequenced cell populations revealed that biological replicates grouped together and that samples were segregated by cell type (basal vs suprabasal) in the first component, and by age in the second component (E14.5 vs E16.5).
evidence: This is shown in the PCA plot in Figure 1E.

claim: Intermediate cells at E14.5 and spinous cells at E16.5 are distinct populations.
source: Notably, ICs at E14.5 and spinous cells at E16.5 were not clustered together, indicating that they are distinct populations, as are their corresponding basal cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown by PCA analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: The IC gene signature consisted of 610 genes.
source: The IC gene signature consisted of 610 genes and included Scara5, a scavenger receptor, St8sia6, which encodes a sialyltransferase enzyme, and Tgm1 (transglutaminase 1), an enzyme involved in covalent cross-linking of proteins (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq differential expression analysis.

claim: The IC gene signature includes Scara5, a scavenger receptor.
source: The IC gene signature consisted of 610 genes and included Scara5, a scavenger receptor, St8sia6, which encodes a sialyltransferase enzyme, and Tgm1 (transglutaminase 1), an enzyme involved in covalent cross-linking of proteins (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data and validated by RNAscope.

claim: The IC gene signature includes St8sia6, which encodes a sialyltransferase enzyme.
source: The IC gene signature consisted of 610 genes and included Scara5, a scavenger receptor, St8sia6, which encodes a sialyltransferase enzyme, and Tgm1 (transglutaminase 1), an enzyme involved in covalent cross-linking of proteins (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data and validated by RNAscope and immunofluorescence.

claim: The IC gene signature includes Tgm1 (transglutaminase 1), an enzyme involved in covalent cross-linking of proteins.
source: The IC gene signature consisted of 610 genes and included Scara5, a scavenger receptor, St8sia6, which encodes a sialyltransferase enzyme, and Tgm1 (transglutaminase 1), an enzyme involved in covalent cross-linking of proteins (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data and validated by immunofluorescence.

claim: Scara5 mRNA is detected in intermediate cells but not in suprabasal cells at E16.5.
source: To validate these candidates, we performed RNAscope and detected mRNA of Scara5 and St8sia6 in ICs but not in suprabasal cells at E16.5 (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 2B and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: St8sia6 mRNA is detected in intermediate cells but not in suprabasal cells at E16.5.
source: To validate these candidates, we performed RNAscope and detected mRNA of Scara5 and St8sia6 in ICs but not in suprabasal cells at E16.5 (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2E.

claim: Scara5 expression is specific to intermediate cells.
source: Scara5 expression was specific to ICs, while St8sia6 mRNA was also present in granular cells at E16.5 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 2B-C.

claim: St8sia6 mRNA is present in granular cells at E16.5.
source: Scara5 expression was specific to ICs, while St8sia6 mRNA was also present in granular cells at E16.5 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 2C.

claim: St8sia6 protein is detected in the granular layers at E16.5 but not in intermediate cells at E14.5.
source: In contrast, St8sia6 protein was detected in the granular layers at E16.5 by antibody staining; however, it was not seen in ICs at E14.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Some granular genes are transcriptionally enriched in intermediate cells but not yet appreciably expressed at the protein level.
source: This suggests that some granular genes are transcriptionally enriched in ICs but not yet appreciably expressed at the protein level.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between mRNA and protein levels for St8sia6 and loricrin.

claim: Loricrin expression is detected in intermediate cells, but its protein product is only found in granular cells.
source: This included loricrin, whose expression was detected in ICs, but whose protein product was only found in granular cells.
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Tgm1 protein is present in intermediate cells.
source: We also observed that another protein marker of granular cells, Tgm1, was also present in ICs, as described in more detail below (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4C.

claim: The spinous cell gene signature consisted of 163 genes.
source: There were 163 genes whose transcripts were specifically upregulated in spinous cells at E16.5 (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq differential expression analysis.

claim: MafB is a transcription factor implicated in epidermal differentiation in cultured human epidermal cells.
source: Among this list, the transcription factor MafB was a prominent candidate since it has been implicated in epidermal differentiation in cultured human epidermal cells (Lopez-Pajares et al., 2015), and it is expressed in suprabasal cells in vivo during development (Miyai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MafB is expressed in suprabasal cells in vivo during development.
source: Among this list, the transcription factor MafB was a prominent candidate since it has been implicated in epidermal differentiation in cultured human epidermal cells (Lopez-Pajares et al., 2015), and it is expressed in suprabasal cells in vivo during development (Miyai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation and confirmed by immunofluorescence data in the manuscript.

claim: MafB is present in the first suprabasal cell layers in the epidermis at E16.5 but excluded from granular cells.
source: Consistent with our transcriptional data, immunofluorescence staining of MafB at E16.5 revealed that it was present in the first suprabasal cell layers in the epidermis but was excluded from granular cells (Figure 2 G,I), and it was undetectable in ICs at E14.5.
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2G and quantified in Figure 2I.

claim: MafB is undetectable in intermediate cells at E14.5.
source: Consistent with our transcriptional data, immunofluorescence staining of MafB at E16.5 revealed that it was present in the first suprabasal cell layers in the epidermis but was excluded from granular cells (Figure 2 G,I), and it was undetectable in ICs at E14.5.
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2G.

claim: Cox1 is enriched in spinous cells but not in intermediate cells at the protein level.
source: Another highly upregulated gene in this list, Ptgs1, which encodes the enzyme Cox1, was also enriched in spinous cells but not in ICs at the protein level (Figure 2H and J).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2H and quantified in Figure 2J.

claim: MafB and Cox1 are specific markers for spinous cells in the embryonic epidermis.
source: Therefore, MafB and Cox1 are specific markers for spinous cells in the embryonic epidermis.
evidence: This is concluded from the immunofluorescence data showing their specific expression in spinous cells.

claim: MafB expression is sufficient to decrease cell proliferation in intermediate cells.
source: Examination of EdU incorporation revealed that HA+ cells had a significantly lower rate of incorporation than ICs in controls, demonstrating that MafB expression is sufficient to decrease cell proliferation (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is shown by EdU incorporation data in Figure 3A-B.

claim: There is increased proliferation of surrounding MafB-negative cells in K10-MafB mutant embryos.
source: Notably, however, we found that there was increased proliferation of surrounding MafB-negative cells in mutant embryos (Figure 3A and B), while the overall suprabasal proliferation rate was not significantly different in mutants vs controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by EdU incorporation data in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The overall suprabasal proliferation rate is not significantly different in K10-MafB mutants vs controls.
source: Notably, however, we found that there was increased proliferation of surrounding MafB-negative cells in mutant embryos (Figure 3A and B), while the overall suprabasal proliferation rate was not significantly different in mutants vs controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a homeostatic mechanism for maintaining total proliferation during the epidermal stratification process.
source: This suggests a potential homeostatic mechanism for maintaining total proliferation during the epidermal stratification process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that overall proliferation remains constant despite changes in individual cell populations.

claim: MafB expression decreases the levels of Tgm1 protein in intermediate cells.
source: While we found a decrease in the levels of Tgm1 protein, Scara5 mRNA levels were unchanged (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3C-D.

claim: MafB expression does not change Scara5 mRNA levels in intermediate cells.
source: While we found a decrease in the levels of Tgm1 protein, Scara5 mRNA levels were unchanged (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 3E-F.

claim: MafB may repress parts of the IC signature but does not globally repress all markers.
source: These data demonstrate that MafB may repress parts of the IC signature but does not globally repress all markers.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effects of MafB on different IC markers.

claim: MafB expression is not sufficient to induce the spinous marker Cox1.
source: However, we found that the spinous marker Cox1 was not induced by MafB (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3G-H.

claim: MafB is sufficient for some aspects of spinous fate (like loss of proliferation), but not for the expression of all spinous marker genes.
source: Therefore, MafB is sufficient for some aspects of spinous fate (like loss of proliferation), but not for the expression of all spinous marker genes.
evidence: This is concluded from the partial effects of MafB on spinous cell characteristics.

claim: Categories uniquely enriched in intermediate cells at E14.5 include pathways involved in lipid metabolic processes and establishment of the skin barrier.
source: Categories that were uniquely enriched in ICs at E14.5 included pathways involved in lipid metabolic processes and establishment of the skin barrier (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown by Gene Ontology analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: Lipid metabolic processes and establishment of the skin barrier are hallmarks of granular cells.
source: These pathways are hallmarks of granular cells, which produce and secrete lipids that contribute to the formation of the watertight cornified layer that acts as the epidermal barrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge about granular cell function.

claim: Granular cells produce and secrete lipids that contribute to the formation of the watertight cornified layer that acts as the epidermal barrier.
source: These pathways are hallmarks of granular cells, which produce and secrete lipids that contribute to the formation of the watertight cornified layer that acts as the epidermal barrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge about granular cell function.

claim: Over one-third of the genes in the IC signature are also part of the granular cell signature.
source: Comparing the IC gene signature to a granular gene signature that we generated from published data (Matsui et al., 2021; GSE168011) revealed a striking overlap with over one-third of the genes in the IC signature also being part of the granular cell signature (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by Venn diagram analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: The spinous gene signature overlap with granular cells is just under 20%.
source: In contrast, the spinous gene signature overlap with granular cells was just under 20%.
evidence: This is shown by Venn diagram analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: GO analysis of IC/granular shared genes revealed pathways such as keratinocyte differentiation, endomembrane system, and lipid processes.
source: GO analysis of IC/granular shared genes revealed pathways such as keratinocyte differentiation, endomembrane system (reminiscent of lamellar bodies), and lipid processes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by Gene Ontology analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Grhl3 and Hopx are upregulated in both intermediate cells and granular cells.
source: Notably, both Grhl3 and Hopx, two transcription factors that control late epidermal differentiation, were upregulated in both of these cell types (Chalmers et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2019; Obarzanek-Fojt et al., 2011; Ting et al., 2005a; Ting et al., 2005b; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Grhl3 and Hopx are transcription factors that control late epidermal differentiation.
source: Notably, both Grhl3 and Hopx, two transcription factors that control late epidermal differentiation, were upregulated in both of these cell types (Chalmers et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2019; Obarzanek-Fojt et al., 2011; Ting et al., 2005a; Ting et al., 2005b; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tgm1 is an enzyme that performs protein cross-linking of structural proteins for cornified envelope formation.
source: To validate the expression of canonical granular markers in ICs, we performed immunofluorescence staining of Tgm1, an enzyme that performs protein cross-linking of structural proteins for cornified envelope formation, and Abca12, which plays a role in transporting lipids into lamellar bodies and is disrupted in harlequin ichthyosis (Akiyama, 2010; Thomas et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Tgm1 function supported by citations.

claim: Abca12 plays a role in transporting lipids into lamellar bodies and is disrupted in harlequin ichthyosis.
source: To validate the expression of canonical granular markers in ICs, we performed immunofluorescence staining of Tgm1, an enzyme that performs protein cross-linking of structural proteins for cornified envelope formation, and Abca12, which plays a role in transporting lipids into lamellar bodies and is disrupted in harlequin ichthyosis (Akiyama, 2010; Thomas et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Abca12 function supported by citations.

claim: Tgm1 and Abca12 are expressed at the protein level in intermediate cells, but not in spinous cells.
source: Both proteins were already expressed at the protein level in ICs, but not in spinous cells (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4C-F.

claim: At E15.5, H2B-GFP+ cells labeled at E14.5 are separated from basal cells by a layer of H2B-GFP-negative cells.
source: We followed the H2B-GFP+ cells over time, and we found that at E15.5, these cells were already more superficial, separated from basal cells by a layer of H2B-GFP-negative cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown by lineage tracing data in Figure 5A.

claim: The H2B-GFP-negative cells separating labeled ICs from basal cells at E15.5 are the first spinous cells produced based on their expression of MafB.
source: Based on their expression of MafB, these cells are the first spinous cells produced (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown by co-staining with MafB in Figure 5A.

claim: About 95% of H2B-GFP+ cells at E15.5 (labeled at E14.5) do not stain for MafB.
source: Strikingly, about 95% of H2B-GFP+ cells did not stain for MafB (Figure 5A').
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5A'.

claim: Labeled intermediate cells are displaced upward rather than converting to a spinous cell fate.
source: Thus, rather than converting to a spinous cell fate, they are displaced upward.
evidence: This is inferred from the lineage tracing data showing ICs moving to upper layers without expressing MafB.

claim: At E16.5, H2B-GFP+ cells labeled at E14.5 are located in the uppermost layers of the epidermis.
source: When we chased these cells until E16.5, they were located in the uppermost layers of the epidermis (Figure 5B), and they co-stained with loricrin, a granular cell marker (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by lineage tracing data in Figure 5B.

claim: H2B-GFP+ cells labeled at E14.5 co-stain with loricrin at E16.5.
source: When we chased these cells until E16.5, they were located in the uppermost layers of the epidermis (Figure 5B), and they co-stained with loricrin, a granular cell marker (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Most intermediate cells transition into granular cells without going through a MafB+ state.
source: This indicates that most ICs transition into granular cells without going through a MafB+ state.
evidence: This is concluded from the lineage tracing experiments.

claim: At E18.5, GFP signal from cells labeled at E14.5 is present in the cornified layer.
source: When labeled cells were chased until E18.5, GFP signal was clearly present in the cornified layer, demonstrating that the traced ICs had terminally differentiated before birth (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by lineage tracing data in Figure 5C.

claim: Traced intermediate cells had terminally differentiated before birth.
source: When labeled cells were chased until E18.5, GFP signal was clearly present in the cornified layer, demonstrating that the traced ICs had terminally differentiated before birth (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of labeled cells in the cornified layer.

claim: The first spinous cells arise from basal cells and not from differentiation of intermediate cells.
source: The above data suggest that the first spinous cells arise from basal cells and not from differentiation of ICs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lineage tracing data showing ICs do not become spinous cells.

claim: 80% of basal cells at E15.5 are H2B-GFP+ when labeled at E14.5.
source: In embryos chased to E15.5, we observed that 80% of basal cells and 70% of all MafB+ cells were H2B-GFP+, demonstrating that most spinous cells arise from basal divisions (Figure 5D and D').
evidence: This is shown by lineage tracing data in Figure 5D'.

claim: 70% of all MafB+ cells at E15.5 are H2B-GFP+ when basal cells are labeled at E14.5.
source: In embryos chased to E15.5, we observed that 80% of basal cells and 70% of all MafB+ cells were H2B-GFP+, demonstrating that most spinous cells arise from basal divisions (Figure 5D and D').
evidence: This is shown by lineage tracing data in Figure 5D'.

claim: Most spinous cells arise from basal divisions.
source: In embryos chased to E15.5, we observed that 80% of basal cells and 70% of all MafB+ cells were H2B-GFP+, demonstrating that most spinous cells arise from basal divisions (Figure 5D and D').
evidence: This is concluded from the lineage tracing data.

claim: Regulation of cell morphogenesis and the actin cytoskeleton are among the most highly upregulated pathways in intermediate cells compared to spinous cells.
source: GO term analysis revealed that regulation of cell morphogenesis and the actin cytoskeleton were among the most highly upregulated pathways in ICs (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by Gene Ontology analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: Heatmap analysis of the contractome gene set demonstrates clear differences in suprabasal cell expression at E14.5 and E16.5.
source: Heatmap analysis of the contractome gene set Zaidel-Bar et al., 2015 demonstrated clear differences in suprabasal cell expression at E14.5 and E16.5 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown by heatmap analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: F-actin levels are higher in basal and suprabasal cells at E14.5, as well as in granular cells at E16.5, but low in spinous cells at E16.5.
source: We observed that F-actin levels were higher in basal and suprabasal cells at E14.5, as well as in granular cells at E16.5. However, they were low in spinous cells at this later time point (Figure 6C–C'').
evidence: This is shown by phalloidin staining in Figure 6C-C''.

claim: Myosin IIA is higher in intermediate cells than spinous cells.
source: Myosin IIA, a major contributor to actomyosin contractility in the epidermis (Miroshnikova et al., 2018; Sumigray et al., 2012), was also higher in ICs than spinous cells (Figure 6D–D'').
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence staining in Figure 6D-D''.

claim: Myosin IIA is a major contributor to actomyosin contractility in the epidermis.
source: Myosin IIA, a major contributor to actomyosin contractility in the epidermis (Miroshnikova et al., 2018; Sumigray et al., 2012), was also higher in ICs than spinous cells (Figure 6D–D'').
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: α18 antibody recognizes an epitope of α-catenin that is exposed when adherens junctions are under tension.
source: Similarly, α18, an antibody that recognizes an epitope of α-catenin that is exposed when adherens junctions are under tension (Yonemura et al., 2010), was also higher in basal and suprabasal cells at E14.5 vs E16.5 (Figure 6E–E'').
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: α18 staining is higher in basal and suprabasal cells at E14.5 vs E16.5.
source: Similarly, α18, an antibody that recognizes an epitope of α-catenin that is exposed when adherens junctions are under tension (Yonemura et al., 2010), was also higher in basal and suprabasal cells at E14.5 vs E16.5 (Figure 6E–E'').
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence staining in Figure 6E-E''.

claim: Active nuclear YAP is present in intermediate cells and granular cells at E16.5, but not in spinous cells.
source: Furthermore, active nuclear YAP, a mechanoresponsive transcriptional co-activator, was present in ICs and granular cells at E16.5, but not in spinous cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence staining in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: YAP is a mechanoresponsive transcriptional co-activator.
source: Furthermore, active nuclear YAP, a mechanoresponsive transcriptional co-activator, was present in ICs and granular cells at E16.5, but not in spinous cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about YAP function.

claim: The percentage of basal cells at E14.5 with active YAP is significantly higher than basal cells at E16.5.
source: Similarly, the percentage of basal cells at E14.5 with active YAP was significantly higher than basal cells at E16.5.
evidence: This is shown by quantification in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The active form of YAP is an important driver of proliferation in the basal layers of the epidermis.
source: Apart from its role in mechanotransduction, the active form of YAP is an important driver of proliferation in the basal layers of the epidermis (Aragona et al., 2020; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Active YAP is not sufficient to induce proliferation in spinous cells.
source: Active YAP was not sufficient to induce proliferation in spinous cells; however, it resulted in a non-cell autonomous increase in proliferation of basal cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by EdU incorporation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Active YAP results in a non-cell autonomous increase in proliferation of basal cells.
source: Active YAP was not sufficient to induce proliferation in spinous cells; however, it resulted in a non-cell autonomous increase in proliferation of basal cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by EdU incorporation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: 47% of contractility-induced genes overlap with the granular gene signature.
source: Remarkably, we found that 47% of contractility-induced genes overlapped with the granular gene signature (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating a major change in gene expression and differentiation state by intracellular contractility (hypergeometric test representation factor 3.4, p=2 × 10–101).
evidence: This is shown by Venn diagram analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The common signature between contractility-induced genes and granular genes is highly enriched in keratinocyte differentiation, cornified envelope, lamellar bodies, and lipid processes.
source: GO analysis revealed that the common signature was highly enriched in keratinocyte differentiation, cornified envelope, lamellar bodies, and lipid processes – all hallmarks of granular cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown by Gene Ontology analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: 80 of the 610 genes in the IC signature (13%) are also found in the contractile signature.
source: When comparing with the IC signature, there was still significant overlap – 80 of the 610 genes in the IC signature (13%) were also found in the contractile signature, though less than that found in the granular cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by Venn diagram analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The overlapping genes between ICs and the contractile gene signature include the late epidermal differentiation transcriptional regulators Grhl3 and Hopx.
source: These included the late epidermal differentiation transcriptional regulators Grhl3 and Hopx.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the overlapping gene sets.

claim: The most enriched terms for the overlapping genes between ICs and the contractile gene signature are lipid processing and transport.
source: The most enriched terms for the overlapping genes between ICs and the contractile gene signature were lipid processing and transport (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown by Gene Ontology analysis in Figure 7B.

claim: Mainly lipid metabolic genes are upregulated in the shared ICs, granular cells, and contractility signatures.
source: In addition, mainly lipid metabolic genes were upregulated in the shared ICs, granular cells, and contractility signatures (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that these were the pathways commonly upregulated in ICs and granular cells as a consequence of contractility.
evidence: This is shown by Gene Ontology analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Many EDC genes are enriched in the contractile and granular signatures, but many fewer in the IC signature.
source: Notably, many EDC genes were enriched in the contractile and granular signatures, but many fewer in the IC signature (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression data.

claim: The contractile gene signature is much more similar to the full granular gene expression program than the IC signature.
source: This demonstrates specific differentiation pathways are enriched in ICs, while the contractile gene signature is much more similar to the full granular gene expression program.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of gene signature overlaps.

claim: Suprabasal cells with increased contractility do not express the spinous marker MafB.
source: In both mouse models, suprabasal cells with increased contractility (at E16.5 and later) did not express the spinous marker MafB (Figure 7C and E), even when they were positioned in the first layers on top of basal cells, where they should clearly be spinous cells.
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7C and E.

claim: Suprabasal cells with increased contractility precociously express the granular marker Tgm1.
source: In contrast, these cells precociously expressed the granular marker Tgm1 (Figure 7D and F).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7D and F.

claim: The effects of increased suprabasal contractility are the same regardless of the time of its induction.
source: These latter results suggest that the effects of increased suprabasal contractility are the same regardless of the time of its induction.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments inducing contractility at different developmental stages.

claim: Increasing suprabasal contractility does not alter Scara5 mRNA levels in HA+ cells compared to controls.
source: Analysis of the IC marker Scara5 revealed that increasing suprabasal contractility did not alter Scara5 mRNA levels in HA+ cells compared to controls, suggesting that contractility induces a granular-like rather than intermediate-like cell type in mutant mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 7G.

claim: Contractility induces a granular-like rather than intermediate-like cell type in mutant mice.
source: Analysis of the IC marker Scara5 revealed that increasing suprabasal contractility did not alter Scara5 mRNA levels in HA+ cells compared to controls, suggesting that contractility induces a granular-like rather than intermediate-like cell type in mutant mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of IC marker expression in hypercontractile cells.

claim: YAP concentrates within the nucleus in suprabasal epidermal cells in both K10-Spastin and K10-Arhgef11CA mouse models.
source: YAP concentrates within the nucleus in suprabasal epidermal cells in both of our mouse models that increase contractility (Ning et al., 2021), and YAP is also localized to the nucleus in granular cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Inducing active YAP does not induce Tgm1 in spinous cells.
source: We observed that inducing active YAP did not induce Tgm1 in spinous cells and did not suppress the expression of MafB, the spinous cell marker (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inducing active YAP does not suppress the expression of MafB.
source: We observed that inducing active YAP did not induce Tgm1 in spinous cells and did not suppress the expression of MafB, the spinous cell marker (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: YAP activation lies downstream of contractility but is not sufficient to induce the effects observed by increased contractility in spinous cells.
source: These data suggest that YAP activation lies downstream of contractility but is not sufficient to induce the effects observed by increased contractility in spinous cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of active YAP on differentiation markers.

claim: Stretching of keratinocytes results in epigenetic changes, including an increase in H3K27me3 levels.
source: In addition to YAP activation, stretching of keratinocytes results in epigenetic changes, including an increase in H3K27me3 levels (Le et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Inducing contractility does not cause a significant change in nuclear levels of H3K27me3.
source: However, inducing contractility did not cause a significant change in nuclear levels of this epigenetic mark (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown by quantification in Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: Basal cells undergo significant changes between E14.5 and E16.5.
source: This revealed that basal cells undergo significant changes between E14.5 and E16.5, consistent with the fact that they generate distinct cell progeny at these time points (ICs vs spinous cells).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis showing transcriptional differences.

claim: Basal cells at E14.5 and E16.5 show differences in mechanical properties.
source: In addition, like suprabasal cells, basal cells at these time points also show differences in mechanical properties.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining of contractility markers.

claim: The IC transcriptome is especially enriched for lipid-modifying enzymes that play a key role in barrier formation.
source: This gene expression program was especially enriched for lipid-modifying enzymes that play a key role in barrier formation.
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis of the IC signature.

claim: Lipids are synthesized in granular cells and stored in lamellar bodies before secreting them to the intercellular spaces.
source: Lipids are synthesized in granular cells and stored in lamellar bodies before secreting them to the intercellular spaces (Prado-Mantilla and Lechler, 2023; Vietri Rudan and Watt, 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The lipid synthesis process may begin early in intermediate cells.
source: Our data suggest that this process may begin early in ICs.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of lipid-related genes in ICs.

claim: Few EDC genes are upregulated in intermediate cells.
source: In contrast, few EDC genes were upregulated in ICs, suggesting that only parts of the granular program are expressed early in these cells, and many of the structural components of the eventual barrier are expressed only later.
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Only parts of the granular program are expressed early in intermediate cells.
source: In contrast, few EDC genes were upregulated in ICs, suggesting that only parts of the granular program are expressed early in these cells, and many of the structural components of the eventual barrier are expressed only later.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective expression of granular genes in ICs.

claim: Many of the structural components of the eventual barrier are expressed only later in development.
source: In contrast, few EDC genes were upregulated in ICs, suggesting that only parts of the granular program are expressed early in these cells, and many of the structural components of the eventual barrier are expressed only later.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal expression patterns of EDC genes.

claim: There are two distinct differentiation pathways leading to the granular cell state, one through ICs during development and one through spinous cells postnatally.
source: This reveals two distinct differentiation pathways leading to the granular cell state, one through ICs during development and one through spinous cells postnatally.
evidence: This is concluded from the lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Actomyosin regulators are transcriptionally upregulated in both intermediate cells and granular cells as compared to spinous cells.
source: Actomyosin regulators were transcriptionally upregulated in both of these cell types as compared to spinous cells, and we were able to validate these findings in intact skin.
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data and validated by immunofluorescence.

claim: Contractility is sufficient to induce granular-like gene expression and to repress some spinous cell markers.
source: Importantly, we found that contractility was sufficient to induce granular-like gene expression and to repress some spinous cell markers.
evidence: This is shown by experiments using K10-Spastin and K10-Arhgef11CA mouse models.

claim: Contractility lies upstream, as well as presumably downstream, of differentiation pathways.
source: This reveals a rather direct effect of contractility lying upstream, as well as presumably downstream, of differentiation pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the bidirectional relationship between contractility and differentiation.

claim: Increased contractility results in premature formation of the epidermal barrier.
source: It also explains the observation that increased contractility results in premature formation of the epidermal barrier (Muroyama and Lechler, 2017; Ning et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Granular cells have increased actomyosin contractility, which is important for the function and placement of tight junctions specifically in this layer of the epidermis.
source: It has been appreciated for some time that granular cells have increased actomyosin contractility, which is important for the function and placement of tight junctions specifically in this layer of the epidermis (Itoh et al., 2012; Prado-Mantilla and Lechler, 2023; Rübsam et al., 2017; Sumigray et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The epidermis increases contractility in response to externally applied forces that result in stretch.
source: The epidermis increases contractility in response to externally applied forces that result in stretch and in response to perturbation of cell adhesions (Aragona et al., 2020; Sumigray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The epidermis increases contractility in response to perturbation of cell adhesions.
source: The epidermis increases contractility in response to externally applied forces that result in stretch and in response to perturbation of cell adhesions (Aragona et al., 2020; Sumigray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Contractility has a strong effect on the EDC.
source: Of note, we found that contractility had a strong effect on the EDC, whose positioning within the nucleus changes with differentiation (Gdula et al., 2013; Mardaryev et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data showing upregulation of EDC genes in hypercontractile cells.

claim: The positioning of the EDC within the nucleus changes with differentiation.
source: Of note, we found that contractility had a strong effect on the EDC, whose positioning within the nucleus changes with differentiation (Gdula et al., 2013; Mardaryev et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Aspects of epigenetics and chromatin organization may be downstream of contractility.
source: This suggests that aspects of epigenetics and chromatin organization may be downstream of contractility, as shown by external forces directly stretching chromatin (Tajik et al., 2016) and extrinsic topographical cues constricting the nucleus to induce chromatin reprogramming (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is speculated based on previous literature showing effects of mechanical forces on chromatin.

claim: External forces can directly stretch chromatin.
source: This suggests that aspects of epigenetics and chromatin organization may be downstream of contractility, as shown by external forces directly stretching chromatin (Tajik et al., 2016) and extrinsic topographical cues constricting the nucleus to induce chromatin reprogramming (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Extrinsic topographical cues can constrict the nucleus to induce chromatin reprogramming.
source: This suggests that aspects of epigenetics and chromatin organization may be downstream of contractility, as shown by external forces directly stretching chromatin (Tajik et al., 2016) and extrinsic topographical cues constricting the nucleus to induce chromatin reprogramming (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: There is a decrease in mRNA levels of Sun1 and Nesprin1/3 in hypercontractile cells.
source: Notably, we found that there is a decrease in mRNA levels of Sun1 and Nesprin1/3, parts of a complex that tether the actin cytoskeleton in the cytoplasm to chromatin in the nucleus when contractility is increased, in hypercontractile cells.
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data from hypercontractile cells.

claim: Sun1 and Nesprin1/3 are parts of a complex that tether the actin cytoskeleton in the cytoplasm to chromatin in the nucleus.
source: Notably, we found that there is a decrease in mRNA levels of Sun1 and Nesprin1/3, parts of a complex that tether the actin cytoskeleton in the cytoplasm to chromatin in the nucleus when contractility is increased, in hypercontractile cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the LINC complex.

claim: Loss of Sun1/2 leads to precocious differentiation in the epidermis.
source: Loss of Sun1/2 also leads to precocious differentiation in the epidermis (Carley et al., 2021) through effects on integrin-mediated mechanical integration, though whether regulation of these connections mediates the contractility effect seen in suprabasal cells will require further investigation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.
